title: 512 bytes at a time: reconstructing IBM i save-file checksums
content_html:
Intro

What exactly must be recalculated when bytes inside an IBM i save file are modified?

IBM i save files, usually called SAVFs, use two container-consistency checksum mechanisms. Every 512-byte payload has a 16-byte trailer, and the logical stream also carries a 16-byte global checksum in its final payload. I wanted to understand both mechanisms well enough to reproduce them, modify a SAVF, and repair only the bytes that depended on my change.

For the reconstruction, I used a small IBM-generated SAVF and the publicly distributed jSAVF reader, whose JAR I decompiled. I reimplemented both algorithms in Python and reproduced every stored checksum in the original file. A second file contained three changed payload bytes and a stale global checksum. Repairing that container changed only the global-checksum field and the final record trailer. I also found the global algorithm’s table and adjacent constants in IBM i Licensed Internal Code (LIC) installation media.

Finally, I used the reconstructed format to remove one complete object from a two-object SAVF. A copy with valid record trailers but a stale global checksum was rejected during import. After I regenerated the global checksum and final trailer, IBM i accepted the shorter SAVF, DSPSAVF showed only the retained object, and that unchanged object restored successfully.

These values provide internal consistency checks for the SAVF container, but they are deterministic, unkeyed, and recomputable. They do not authenticate the source or prevent somebody from modifying a file and recalculating its checksums. IBM i has separate mechanisms for SAVF signatures and for validating the objects stored inside the container. I will return to that boundary after the reversing work.

Building a SAVF I could modify

I wanted a small SAVF whose contents I controlled, so I created one containing a disposable program named USERB1/CALLAES. I disabled data compression because fixed, uncompressed payloads are much easier to compare byte for byte:

CRTSAVF FILE(USERB1/SAVE1)
SAVOBJ OBJ(CALLAES) LIB(USERB1) OBJTYPE(*PGM) DEV(*SAVF) SAVF(USERB1/SAVE1) DTACPR(*NO)

CRTSAVF creates the save-file object. SAVOBJ saves the program into it, and DTACPR(*NO) keeps the data uncompressed. It does not disable either checksum layer.

I copied the SAVF directly from /QSYS.LIB over SCP:

scp userb1@ibmi.example:/QSYS.LIB/USERB1.LIB/SAVE1.FILE .

The /QSYS.LIB/USERB1.LIB/SAVE1.FILE path is the Integrated File System view of the SAVF object. This transfer gives me a binary file that I can inspect byte for byte.

The resulting SAVE1.FILE is 84,480 bytes long.

What a SAVF looks like

I did not have to discover the outer record format from scratch. A January 2001 MI400 post describes RISC SAVFs as 528-byte records: 512 data bytes, a four-byte binary record number, and a 12-byte checksum. A 2007 midrange.com discussion also describes checksum information in each 528-byte record.

That layout fits my test file exactly:

84,480 bytes = 160 * 528

Each physical record contains a 512-byte payload followed by a 16-byte trailer:

physical file:  | 512-byte payload | 16-byte trailer | 512-byte payload | ...
logical stream: |         512 payload bytes         |         512 payload bytes

Removing the trailers leaves an 81,920-byte logical stream:

81,920 bytes = 160 * 512

Once those trailers are removed, an offset inside the logical SAVF stream no longer matches the corresponding raw-file offset. I therefore use two coordinate systems:

  • a physical offset addresses the transferred file, including the trailers;
  • a logical offset addresses the concatenated 512-byte payloads.

The conversion is:

def logical_to_physical(offset: int) -> int:
    return (offset // 512) * 528 + (offset % 512)

A modified copy named SAVE2.FILE appears later in the experiment. Its three payload differences from SAVE1.FILE show why this distinction matters:

Logical offset Record index Offset in payload Physical offset
0x6D50 54 0x150 0x70B0
0x6D52 54 0x152 0x70B2
0x6D53 54 0x153 0x70B3

Here, index 54 means the zero-based record index. The trailer stores a one-based sequence, so the same unit is record #55. Hex editors and cmp use physical offsets; structures inside the SAVF use logical offsets.

IBM also documents part of this outer layer. The CRTSAVF documentation says that retrieved SAVF records carry sequencing checksum information. IBM i validates it when records are inserted and rejects changed or out-of-sequence records. That documentation covers per-record insertion checks, not the global checksum discussed later.

I did not run a separate live negative control for a corrupted record trailer. Record-level enforcement is documented by IBM; the controlled negative experiment later in this article isolates the second mechanism, the global checksum.

Other public work already covered more than the outer layout. The initial 9 August 2026 revision of the Try-AS/400 SAVF page, preserved as revision 1781 in its page history, documented the per-record folding, timestamp XOR, global overlay, and backup at logical 0x40. It also documented the header-length and record-count fields, the item marker, name, catalogue reference, stored and total lengths, and the QSYS catalogue’s object count and descriptor layout used by the removal experiment below. The page warns that some material was generated or amended by AI and has not been checked, so I credit it as prior public documentation and validate the fields independently against my fixture and jSAVF.

This article focuses on the complete global state-machine order, tests with nonzero backups, the matching LIC data, deterministic reconstruction and repair, public test vectors, and controlled IBM i behavior.

Reconstructing the per-record checksum

Instead of guessing standard checksum families, I looked for an existing SAVF reader. jSAVF already implemented the format, and its author credits information from the archive.midrange.com community, especially for IBM’s two proprietary checksum algorithms. I decompiled the distributed JAR and used its ChunkChecker logic as the starting point for the per-record algorithm.

The first four bytes of each 16-byte trailer are the one-based record sequence. The remaining 12 bytes are the transformed checksum value. The values are easy to see in SAVE1.FILE:

index 0   / record #1:   00000001 8f40b6a68e88a98ea91e2d60
index 1   / record #2:   00000002 af2012d24b4b7f2000004000
index 159 / record #160: 000000a0 afc501282b18f73c5c308e69

The decompiled code also uses the first eight bytes of the SAVF when building every record checksum. In SAVE1.FILE, those bytes are:

af2012d24b4b7f20

jSAVF treats this value as the SAVF timestamp and mixes it into the checksum after the reduction passes.

The main operation in the decompiled code is a shifted byte-array addition. jSAVF calls it chkAdd; the Python reconstruction below uses the name chk_add. The destination is one byte longer than the source:

def chk_add(source: bytearray, destination: bytearray) -> None:
    shift_carry = 0
    add_carry = 0

    for i in range(len(source) - 1, -1, -1):
        value = source[i]
        shifted = ((value << 1) | shift_carry) & 0xff
        shift_carry = value >> 7

        total = shifted + destination[i + 1] + add_carry
        add_carry = total >> 8
        destination[i + 1] = total & 0xff

    destination[0] = (
        destination[0] + add_carry + shift_carry
    ) & 0xff

The source and destination are both big-endian bignums — the byte array is just one large number’s digits, most-significant byte first. chk_add doubles the source bignum (shift left by one bit) and adds it into the destination, which is one byte wider to hold any overflow. The bit that overflows out of the source’s top byte, plus the final carry from the addition, both land in destination[0].

The algorithm starts with the four-byte sequence followed by the 512-byte payload. It reduces those 516 bytes in two passes:

Pass Input Buffer lengths Output
1 516 bytes 61 through 68 68 bytes
2 68 bytes 5 through 12 12 bytes

Each pass fills eight buffers and then performs seven cascading chk_add operations. The unusual part is the order of the final two input slices. The first pass fills them in 68, 67 order, and the second uses 12, 11. The accumulator chain still runs through buffer indexes 0 to 7:

def reduce_once(data: bytes, input_sizes: list[int]) -> bytes:
    parts = []
    offset = 0
    for size in input_sizes:
        parts.append(bytearray(data[offset:offset + size]))
        offset += size
    assert offset == len(data)

    # Earlier input fills buffer 7; the final input fills buffer 6.
    accumulators = parts[0:6] + [parts[7], parts[6]]
    for i in range(7):
        chk_add(accumulators[i], accumulators[i + 1])
    return bytes(accumulators[7])

phase1_input = sequence.to_bytes(4, "big") + payload
phase1 = reduce_once(phase1_input, [61, 62, 63, 64, 65, 66, 68, 67])
phase2 = reduce_once(phase1,       [ 5,  6,  7,  8,  9, 10, 12, 11])

The last step XORs the first eight output bytes with the SAVF timestamp and prepends the sequence:

result = bytearray(phase2)
for i in range(8):
    result[i] ^= timestamp[i]

record_checksum = sequence.to_bytes(4, "big") + bytes(result)

Record #2 gives a compact test vector. Its 512-byte payload is entirely zero. With sequence 2 and timestamp af2012d24b4b7f20, the calculation produces:

00000002 af2012d24b4b7f2000004000

That is exactly the trailer stored in the IBM-generated file. Running the same calculation over all 160 records also reproduces every stored trailer.

The zero payload is useful for checking the sequence handling and timestamp XOR, but it does not detect the unusual slice order. Both the correct order and a plain ascending fill produce the same zero-payload result. I therefore added a patterned record vector:

payload = bytes(range(256)) * 2
sequence = 2
timestamp = bytes.fromhex("af2012d24b4b7f20")

The correct 68,67 and 12,11 fill order produces:

000000028e43fa214379304d4081df91

Filling the last two buffers in plain ascending order instead produces:

0000000272b71b3df71e6c4d4081df3f

I checked the correct result directly with jSAVF 1.83’s compiled ChunkChecker, as well as with the public Python implementation used below. This vector catches the ordering error without exposing any bytes from the test SAVF.

Finding the global checksum

Fixing the record trailers was not enough. jSAVF’s GlobalChecker showed a second 16-byte value calculated over the complete logical stream.

The field sits in the final 16 logical bytes. Physically, those are the last 16 bytes of the final record’s payload, immediately before its record trailer:

| 496 ordinary payload bytes | 16-byte global checksum | 16-byte record trailer |
                              ^ file_size - 32           ^ file_size - 16

For my 84,480-byte file, the global field begins at 0x149E0 (84,448) and the final record trailer begins at 0x149F0 (84,464).

This creates a self-reference problem: the global checksum occupies bytes that would otherwise be part of its own input. In the decompiled code, GlobalChecker solves it by reading the original 16 bytes from logical offset 0x40 in the first payload. To calculate the global value, I restore that backup over the final field, process the reconstructed logical stream, and then write the checksum back into the final payload.

The global routine uses a 2,048-byte lookup table. jSAVF stores it as net/anerty/os400/savf/check/sandbox.ser inside the JAR. The file is a serialized Java byte array, 2,075 bytes long, with the actual table beginning at offset 27:

ac ed 00 05 75 72 ... 00 00 08 00 <2,048-byte payload>
^ stream magic                         ^ length = 0x800

The table hash is:

2,048-byte table SHA-256:
93f81fd81523a2521cf17b234edb05155998bc7e46d88b966b4bd9eef64c0764

The table contains eight 256-byte blocks. Each block is a permutation of 00 through ff, so every byte value occurs eight times in the complete table.

I checked the current jSAVF 1.83 distribution and extracted the same resource with these commands:

curl -fL -A 'Mozilla/5.0' -O https://www.anerty.net/dl/jsavf-dist-1.83-jars-only-linux.tar.xz
tar -xJf jsavf-dist-1.83-jars-only-linux.tar.xz
unzip -p jsavf/jSAVF-1.83.jar net/anerty/os400/savf/check/sandbox.ser > sandbox.ser

The global state starts with two eight-byte values and two counters:

s0 = bytearray([0x55] * 8)
s8 = bytearray([0xaa] * 8)
c0 = 1
c8 = 121

Each 512-byte payload is processed as 32 blocks of 16 bytes. The first eight bytes update s0, and the second eight update s8. Each half is treated as a ring of 8 bytes rather than a flat list, so every byte has a neighbor to its right and byte 7 wraps back around to byte 0:

 b0 → b1 → b2 → b3
  ↑             ↓
 b7 ← b6 ← b5 ← b4

Reading clockwise from b7, each adjacent pair feeds one table lookup: (b7,b0) → state[0], (b0,b1) → state[1], … (b6,b7) → state[7]. The routine builds this ring by prepending a copy of the last byte, giving a nine-byte window, then folds each adjacent pair into an 11-bit table index:

window = bytes([half[7]]) + half
for k in range(8):
    index = ((window[k] << 8) | window[k + 1]) & 0x7ff
    state[k] ^= table[index]

After the table XOR, the eight-byte state rotates left by 29 bits as one unsigned big-endian 64-bit value.

When the s0 counter reaches 251 or the s8 counter reaches 257, the corresponding state is shuffled at bit level. An s8 threshold event also exchanges bytes 4 through 7 between the two states.

The following pseudocode includes all state and ordering needed to reproduce the checksum. physical is the complete SAVF image and table is the 2,048-byte lookup table. The function derives the ordered 512-byte payload blocks by stripping the 16-byte physical trailer from each 528-byte record:

MASK64 = (1 << 64) - 1

def rotate_left_64_be(state: bytearray, count: int = 29) -> None:
    value = int.from_bytes(state, "big", signed=False)
    value = ((value << count) | (value >> (64 - count))) & MASK64
    state[:] = value.to_bytes(8, "big")

def build_spread_tables():
    spread1 = [0] * 256
    for byte in range(256):
        value = 0
        for bit in range(7, -1, -1):
            value = (value << 2) | ((byte >> bit) & 1)
        spread1[byte] = value
    spread2 = [(value << 1) & 0xffff for value in spread1]
    return spread1, spread2

def shuffle(state, spread1, spread2):
    output = bytearray(8)
    for pair in range(4):
        value = spread2[state[pair]] | spread1[state[pair + 4]]
        output[pair * 2:pair * 2 + 2] = value.to_bytes(2, "big")
    state[:] = output

def mix_half(half, state, counter, threshold,
             table, spread1, spread2):
    window = bytes([half[7]]) + bytes(half)
    for k in range(8):
        index = ((window[k] << 8) | window[k + 1]) & 0x7ff
        state[k] ^= table[index]

    rotate_left_64_be(state, 29)

    threshold_event = (counter == threshold)
    if threshold_event:
        counter = 0
        shuffle(state, spread1, spread2)

    # The caller performs the cross-state exchange, if required,
    # before incrementing this counter.
    return counter, threshold_event

def compute_global_checksum(physical: bytes, table: bytes) -> bytes:
    assert len(physical) > 0 and len(physical) % 528 == 0
    assert len(table) == 2048

    records = [
        physical[i * 528:i * 528 + 512]
        for i in range(len(physical) // 528)
    ]

    spread1, spread2 = build_spread_tables()
    s0 = bytearray([0x55] * 8)
    s8 = bytearray([0xaa] * 8)
    c0, c8 = 1, 121

    global_backup = records[0][0x40:0x50]

    for record_index, record in enumerate(records):
        payload = bytearray(record)
        if record_index == len(records) - 1:
            payload[496:512] = global_backup

        for offset in range(0, 512, 16):
            block = payload[offset:offset + 16]

            c0, _ = mix_half(
                block[0:8], s0, c0, 251, table, spread1, spread2
            )
            c0 += 1

            c8, s8_event = mix_half(
                block[8:16], s8, c8, 257, table, spread1, spread2
            )
            if s8_event:
                old_s0_tail = bytes(s0[4:8])
                s0[4:8] = s8[4:8]
                s8[4:8] = old_s0_tail
            c8 += 1

    return bytes(s0) + bytes(s8)

build_spread_tables implements a classic bit-interleaving trick: spread1[byte] spreads the 8 bits of byte out so each bit lands in every other bit position of a 16-bit value, leaving the in-between positions zero; spread2 is the same table shifted left by one bit, so its bits land exactly in the positions spread1 left empty:

bit position:   15 14 13 12 11 10 09 08 07 06 05 04 03 02 01 00
spread1(byte):   0 b7  0 b6  0 b5  0 b4  0 b3  0 b2  0 b1  0 b0
spread2(byte):  b7  0 b6  0 b5  0 b4  0 b3  0 b2  0 b1  0 b0  0

shuffle then combines one byte from each half of the state — spread2[state[pair]] from the first half, spread1[state[pair + 4]] from the second — by OR-ing their spread values together, interleaving the two bytes’ bits pairwise into one 16-bit output. Doing this for all four byte pairs interleaves the state’s two four-byte halves together, bit by bit.

The order matters. The algorithm first applies the table XOR and rotates the result by 29 bits. It then tests the counter. If the counter has reached its limit, the algorithm resets it and shuffles the bits. For s8, it also exchanges four bytes between the two running values. Only then does it increment the counter. Changing this order changes the result.

A synthetic global-checksum vector

The following vector tests the global algorithm without a private SAVF. It contains nine physical records. Payload byte i in zero-based record r is (r * 17 + i * 29 + 3) & 0xff. The backup at logical 0x40 is f0f1...feff, the final overlay initially contains a0a1...aeaf, and each 16-byte physical trailer is zero because trailers are not global-checksum input.

Nine records contain 288 blocks, so this vector reaches both shuffle thresholds and the s8-triggered cross-state exchange:

records = []
for record_index in range(9):
    payload = bytearray(
        (record_index * 17 + offset * 29 + 3) & 0xff
        for offset in range(512)
    )
    records.append(payload)

records[0][0x40:0x50] = bytes(range(0xf0, 0x100))
records[-1][496:512] = bytes(range(0xa0, 0xb0))

physical = bytearray()
for payload in records:
    physical.extend(payload)
    physical.extend(bytes(16))

expected = bytes.fromhex("dbf1671ed17396a03f60bd52ddf749db")
calculated = compute_global_checksum(bytes(physical), table)
assert calculated == expected
print(f"calculated global: {calculated.hex()}")

The output is:

calculated global: dbf1671ed17396a03f60bd52ddf749db

The lookup table has the SHA-256 shown above. I checked this expected value directly with jSAVF 1.83’s compiled GlobalChecker and with the independent Python reconstruction.

Why the final record must be repaired last

Writing the global checksum changes the final record’s payload and invalidates that record’s trailer. For an ordinary payload edit, the dependencies are:

changed payload bytes
    +-> affected record trailer(s)
    `-> global checksum
            `-> final record trailer

The global calculation reads only the 512-byte payloads, not the physical record trailers. The affected trailer and the global value are therefore parallel results of the payload change. The final trailer depends on the newly written global value and must be calculated last.

A safe repair order is:

  1. recalculate the record trailers;
  2. calculate the global value after restoring the header backup over the final field;
  3. write the global value at file_size - 32;
  4. recalculate the final record trailer again.

There is one special case. The global field physically replaces the true final 16 logical bytes. If those bytes must change, the replacement data belongs in the backup at logical 0x40. That changes record #1’s payload and trailer, the global checksum, and finally the last record’s trailer.

Testing the backup assumption

The SAVFs used in the main experiment had zero-filled backups at logical 0x40. This meant that an implementation which replaced the final field with zeroes would still produce the correct result for those files. I therefore looked for SAVFs with a nonzero backup and found two useful examples:

File Backup at logical 0x40 Stored global Zero-filled calculation Backup-aware calculation
20260830_QSYS_QTOCSSTBL_uncompressed.savf 40404040404040404040404040404040 d1d0d5c608257c3a75f62b1d3b509364 11101506c8e5bcfab536ebddfb9053a4 exact match
QTOFRULZ.FILE d3404040404000000000000000000000 59311393322093c8527e36d903e5c4a4 99f1d393395a1308527e36d903e5c4a4 exact match

Both files also have valid per-record trailers. Replacing the overlaid field with zeroes produces the wrong values shown in the table. Restoring the 16-byte header backup reproduces each stored global checksum exactly. For these two files, this confirms that the backup is part of the global-checksum input.

Finding the same constants in IBM LIC

jSAVF showed how the global checksum was calculated. I also wanted to see whether the same unusual table and constants appeared in IBM’s LIC.

I searched an IBM i 7.5 RS_750-J Licensed Machine Code installation image for the complete 2,048-byte table. It occurs once in the installation image, at offset 0x42FDE8A0. Within the 64 bytes immediately before the table, I found the two state seeds, both counter seeds, and both thresholds used by the reconstructed algorithm:

0x42FDE860: 55555555 55555555 00000000 00000000   initial s0
0x42FDE870: 00000001 000000fb 00000000 00000000   c0 = 1, threshold = 251
0x42FDE880: aaaaaaaa aaaaaaaa 00000000 00000000   initial s8
0x42FDE890: 00000079 00000101 00000000 00000000   c8 = 121, threshold = 257
0x42FDE8A0: 90aca3f7 e3e620be 686e0935 ea4efd6c   table begins

The same table is present in QFILEMCD, an extracted LIC code-and-data image. It begins at file offset 0x2503E8A0.

If you have access to licensed IBM LIC installation media and an extracted QFILEMCD, the table search itself is straightforward:

from pathlib import Path
import hashlib
import mmap

EXPECTED_TABLE_SHA256 = (
    "93f81fd81523a2521cf17b234edb05155998bc7e46d88b966b4bd9eef64c0764"
)

table_resource = Path("sandbox.ser").read_bytes()
assert len(table_resource) >= 27 + 2048
table = table_resource[27:27 + 2048]
# Pin the table extracted from the jSAVF 1.83 build used for this article.
assert hashlib.sha256(table).hexdigest() == EXPECTED_TABLE_SHA256

with open("QFILEMCD", "rb") as f, \
     mmap.mmap(f.fileno(), 0, access=mmap.ACCESS_READ) as image:
    offsets, start = [], 0
    while (found := image.find(table, start)) != -1:
        offsets.append(found)
        start = found + 1

print([hex(offset) for offset in offsets])

On the QFILEMCD image I analyzed, the output was:

['0x2503e8a0']

This locates one complete copy of the table at the file offset given above.

Finding the constants does not identify the LIC routine that reads them or prove that IBM’s control flow matches jSAVF. It also does not show that the machine which created my SAVF ran this exact LIC level. The search shows that IBM’s installation media contains the same table together with the matching state seeds, counter seeds, and thresholds.

Modifying and repairing the SAVF

I put the backup-aware implementation in a standalone Python script named savf_checksum_demo.py. Its public interface has four operations: repair the checksum fields, list saved objects, copy an object from a compatible donor SAVF, and remove an object. The add and remove operations repair every dependent checksum field automatically. The reproduction section below uses the same object-removal path as the final experiment without requiring private files.

Validating against the original SAVF

I ran the reconstruction on the untouched IBM-generated file. The validation output was:

record trailers: all 160 OK
stored global:     5513f83d38b944fe9814e1dc8d0b04fe
calculated global: 5513f83d38b944fe9814e1dc8d0b04fe
global checksum:   OK

The Python implementation reproduces all 160 record trailers and the stored global value 5513f83d38b944fe9814e1dc8d0b04fe. This checks the record numbering, both reduction passes, timestamp XOR, table parsing, field placement, and global state transitions against values written by IBM i.

Analyzing a valid-record, stale-global file

SAVE2.FILE gave me a useful intermediate state. Compared with SAVE1.FILE, three program payload bytes in record #55 (index 54) changed to 0x41:

Logical offset Physical offset Change
0x6D50 0x70B0 fb to 41
0x6D52 0x70B2 ff to 41
0x6D53 0x70B3 30 to 41

Five bytes in record #55’s trailer changed with the payload. The updated trailer matches those bytes, and all 160 record trailers are valid. The global checksum and the final record trailer are still byte-for-byte equal to SAVE1.FILE, so the stored global value is stale.

record trailers: all 160 OK
stored global:     5513f83d38b944fe9814e1dc8d0b04fe
calculated global: 5013b87d388154fb9835f5dc8d0980ff
global checksum:   STALE

Compared with SAVE1.FILE, this intermediate file differs at eight positions: the three payload bytes and five bytes in record #55’s trailer. I recreated this state by applying those three edits to SAVE1.FILE and recalculating only record #55’s trailer; the result matched SAVE2.FILE byte for byte.

Predicting the repair footprint

The dependency model predicts that repairing SAVE2.FILE should change only two places:

  • the embedded global field;
  • the final record trailer, because the global field is part of its payload.

The changed program bytes and record #55 trailer should remain untouched.

I repaired a copy with the final tool:

$ python3 savf_checksum_demo.py fix SAVE2.FILE SAVE2-repaired.FILE
checksum repaired: SAVE2-repaired.FILE

A separate validation pass found all 160 record trailers valid and both the stored and calculated global value equal to 5013b87d388154fb9835f5dc8d0980ff.

cmp finds exactly 21 changed byte positions between SAVE2.FILE and the repaired output:

physical 0x149E0..0x149EF  global field:          11 positions differ
physical 0x149F0..0x149FF  final record trailer:  10 positions differ
elsewhere:                                           0 differences

Only 11 and 10 positions differ because some bytes happen to be equal in the old and new 16-byte values. The complete comparison is:

Comparison Payload bytes Trailer bytes Global-field bytes Total positions
SAVE1.FILE to SAVE2.FILE 3 5 in record #55 0 8
SAVE2.FILE to repaired output 0 10 in record #160 11 21
SAVE1.FILE to repaired output 3 15 across two trailers 11 29

This is a consistency check rather than an independent validation, because the same implementation both predicts and produces the repair. Still, the output changes only the expected 21 byte positions and nothing else.

Editing a SAVF container

The three-byte SAVE1/SAVE2 comparison established the checksum dependency order, but editing bytes inside a saved program also raises unrelated object-validation questions. For the final test I therefore changed the SAVF structure instead: I removed one complete object from a two-object container and left the retained object’s saved section data unchanged.

I created TESTA and TESTB as disposable copies of the same program and saved them together without compression. The resulting SAVF had 288 physical records. Its backup-restored logical stream contained three sequential items. Here, an item is one continuous area of bytes with its own header and stored length:

QSRDSSPC.1 logical 0x1000..0x3fff length 0x3000 srds 0x0
TESTA      logical 0x4000..0x13fff length 0x10000 srds 0x70
TESTB      logical 0x14000..0x23fff length 0x10000 srds 0x107

In this output, srds is the QSYS catalogue-descriptor offset encoded in the low 24 bits of the item field at +0x24 (zero for the catalogue item itself). A descriptor is the catalogue entry for one saved object.

These offsets come from three different structures, each relative to its own start rather than to the whole file:

logical stream
├─ file header                              (+0x34 header length, +0x08/+0x38 record count)
├─ QSRDSSPC.1 item   0x1000..0x3fff
│    ├─ item header                         (+0x04 name, +0x24 catalogue-descriptor link)
│    └─ catalogue                           (+0x2A object count)
│         ├─ descriptor[0] @ +0x70   (151 bytes — TESTA)
│         └─ descriptor[1] @ +0x107  (151 bytes — TESTB)
├─ TESTA item        0x4000..0x13fff         (item header +0x24 → 0x70)
└─ TESTB item        0x14000..0x23fff        (item header +0x24 → 0x107)

With that in mind: QSRDSSPC.1 is the save/restore data-space item that carries the object catalogue. The parser restores the global overlay before walking the logical stream. The four-byte big-endian header-length field at 0x34 was 0x1000, so the first item began at logical 0x1000. The implementation also supports the documented zero value, which means a 512-byte header. It checks the 0xFFFFFFFF item marker, reads the EBCDIC name at item offset 0x04, and calculates each uncompressed item’s stored length from the four-byte big-endian field at 0x48:

(big_endian_u32(item + 0x48) + 1) * 512

The item also stores its total length, in 512-byte units, in the four-byte big-endian field at 0xCC. The 2001 MI400 description calls this the number of 528-byte records to the next descriptor. Both descriptions agree for contiguous non-final items: the same count describes both views. Multiplying it by 512 gives the item’s logical length, while the same number of 528-byte physical records gives the raw-file distance to the next descriptor. The final item still carries its total length even though no descriptor follows it.

For this fixture, QSRDSSPC.1 stored 0x17 at 0x48 and 0x18 at 0xCC; both derive a length of 0x3000. TESTA and TESTB each stored 0x7F at 0x48 and 0x80 at 0xCC; both derive 0x10000. These values equal the actual item spans. There is no separate absolute next-item pointer in this QSYS layout: the outer parser advances by the computed item length, while the object catalogue is a count-delimited, fixed-stride descriptor array. jSAVF’s separate next-item handling is for IFS catalogue trees, which are not present here.

Removing TESTA did not require changing 0xCC: QSRDSSPC.1 kept its 0x3000 span, and the retained TESTB item moved earlier but kept its 0x10000 span. The editor changed the four-byte big-endian record count at header offset 0x08 and the matching eight-byte big-endian count at 0x38 from 288 to 160; the header-length field remained 0x1000.

The catalogue occupies logical 0x3000..0x3FFF. Its four-byte big-endian object count at catalogue offset 0x2A was two. For this target-release format, the two 151-byte object descriptors began at catalogue offsets 0x70 and 0x107. Each saved-object item contains a four-byte big-endian field at item offset 0x24. jSAVF uses the high byte for IFS flags and the low 24 bits as the QSYS catalogue-descriptor offset; the QSYS values here were 0x70 and 0x107.

Removing TESTA therefore required more than deleting its bytes. The editor:

  1. removed the complete TESTA item at 0x4000..0x13FFF;
  2. changed the catalogue object count from two to one;
  3. moved the TESTB descriptor from 0x107 to 0x70 and cleared the unused slot;
  4. changed TESTB’s item-header descriptor link from 0x107 to 0x70;
  5. updated both record-count fields in the file header;
  6. copied the new final 16 logical bytes to the backup at logical 0x40, rebuilt the physical records, and recalculated every record trailer;
  7. calculated the new global checksum, wrote it to the final payload, and recalculated the final trailer.

The 151-byte TESTB catalogue descriptor was copied unchanged from 0x107 to 0x70. Its header occupation at item offset 0x44 was 0x2F8; its saved-object sections began at the first 4096-byte boundary, item-relative 0x1000. After aligning the baseline and edited TESTB items, the only differences in that first 0x1000-byte descriptor/header area were relative offsets 0x26 and 0x27, inside the four-byte catalogue-reference field. Every byte from item offset 0x1000 through the end of the item was unchanged. The edit produced these structural changes:

Property Baseline Edited
TESTA item 0x4000..0x13FFF absent
TESTB item 0x14000..0x23FFF 0x4000..0x13FFF
Logical size 0x24000 (147,456 bytes) 0x14000 (81,920 bytes)
Physical records 288 160
Physical size 152,064 bytes 84,480 bytes
Stored global checksum 791ea5ec90f35d20829dc5561098c130 bfd84cce59a6e7993e85c8a0e1a4e9cf

For this fixture the new final logical bytes and the backup were both zero. The implementation nevertheless copies the actual new tail into the backup rather than assuming zeroes.

Before import, the repaired result satisfied these invariants:

SAVF differs from baseline: YES
logical structure differs: YES
TESTA present in baseline: YES
TESTA present in edited:   NO
TESTB present in baseline: YES
TESTB present in edited:   YES
TESTB saved-object section payload changed: NO
TESTB item-header descriptor link: 0x107 -> 0x70
record trailers: all 160 OK
stored global == calculated global: YES

I also generated a negative control with the same structural edit and rebuilt record trailers, but left the old global value in place. Its 160 trailers all validated; its stored global was 791ea5ec90f35d20829dc5561098c130, while the calculation produced bfd84cce59a6e7993e85c8a0e1a4e9cf. The stale and repaired copies have identical backup-restored logical streams. Their 28 differing physical byte positions are confined to the global field at 0x149E0..0x149EF and the final record trailer at 0x149F0..0x149FF.

Testing the edited SAVF on IBM i

I transferred the baseline, edited-and-stale, and edited-and-repaired files through the same stream-file and CPYFRMSTMF path on IBM i 7.5. The baseline and edited variants used separate destination SAVFs, and each restore used a fresh target library.

Case Record checks Global CPYFRMSTMF DSPSAVF Restore TESTB
Baseline 288 valid valid CPCA081 TESTA, TESTB CPC3703
Edited + stale 160 valid stale CPDA088, then CPFA095 not reached not reached
Edited + repaired 160 valid valid CPCA081 TESTB only CPC3703

The stale import stopped with:

CPDA088: Error writing to object.
CPFA095: Stream file not copied.

The repaired import completed with:

CPCA081: Stream file copied to object.

DSPSAVF reported 160 records, one saved object, and listed only TESTB. Restoring that retained object into an empty library produced:

CPC3703: 1 objects restored from SVC29 to RMRF29.

The actual controlled run used SVC29 as the source library and RMRF29 as the fresh restore library; the reproduction commands below use generic example names.

This is the practical checksum-fixer result. The SAVF was structurally different, TESTA was absent, and TESTB’s saved-object section data had not changed. After the dependent record and global checksum fields were regenerated, IBM i accepted and interpreted the edited container, and the retained object remained usable.

The editor is not intended to reproduce the byte-for-byte output of a fresh native SAVOBJ operation; the experiment tests whether the structurally edited and checksum-repaired container is accepted and interpreted correctly by IBM i.

Reproducing the experiment

The private research SAVFs are not required. The specific implementation used for these experiments is available in the Silent Signal SAVF IBM i repository. It requires Python 3.9 or later and exposes four commands:

  • fix recalculates every record trailer, the global checksum, and the final trailer;
  • list validates the record trailers and lists the QSYS catalogue;
  • add copies one complete object from a compatible donor SAVF and repairs the output; and
  • remove removes one complete object and repairs the output.

The editor deliberately supports the uncompressed QSYS layout tested here. It rejects compressed items, incompatible catalogues, ambiguous names, unknown links, and insufficient catalogue space rather than guessing.

First extract the lookup-table resource from the public jSAVF distribution:

curl -fL -A 'Mozilla/5.0' -O https://www.anerty.net/dl/jsavf-dist-1.83-jars-only-linux.tar.xz
tar -xJf jsavf-dist-1.83-jars-only-linux.tar.xz
unzip -p jsavf/jSAVF-1.83.jar net/anerty/os400/savf/check/sandbox.ser > sandbox.ser

Every checksum-changing command validates the extracted table against the SHA-256 published earlier in this article before using it.

1. Create and export a two-object baseline

Replace USERB1 with a disposable test library and TESTPGM with a disposable program that can be duplicated. The SSH account and host below are examples.

CRTDUPOBJ OBJ(TESTPGM) FROMLIB(USERB1) OBJTYPE(*PGM) TOLIB(USERB1) NEWOBJ(TESTA)
CRTDUPOBJ OBJ(TESTPGM) FROMLIB(USERB1) OBJTYPE(*PGM) TOLIB(USERB1) NEWOBJ(TESTB)
CRTSAVF FILE(USERB1/BASELINE)
SAVOBJ OBJ(TESTA TESTB) LIB(USERB1) OBJTYPE(*PGM) DEV(*SAVF) SAVF(USERB1/BASELINE) DTACPR(*NO)
CPYTOSTMF FROMMBR('/QSYS.LIB/USERB1.LIB/BASELINE.FILE') TOSTMF('/tmp/baseline.FILE') STMFOPT(*REPLACE)

scp userb1@ibmi.example:/tmp/baseline.FILE baseline.FILE

List the baseline objects, then run a checksum repair into a separate file and compare it with the original:

$ python3 savf_checksum_demo.py list baseline.FILE
TESTA
TESTB

$ python3 savf_checksum_demo.py fix baseline.FILE baseline-checked.FILE
checksum repaired: baseline-checked.FILE

$ cmp -s baseline.FILE baseline-checked.FILE && echo "baseline checksums already valid"
baseline checksums already valid

fix always recalculates the complete checksum state. Byte equality therefore shows that the original already contained the calculated record trailers and global value. Record counts and checksum values depend on the saved objects and IBM i release.

2. Remove one object and repair the container

remove writes a new SAVF, leaves the baseline untouched, and repairs all checksum dependencies in the output:

$ python3 savf_checksum_demo.py remove baseline.FILE edited-repaired.FILE TESTA
removed object: TESTA
objects: TESTB
record count: 288 -> 160

Check the resulting catalogue and prove that a second checksum pass makes no changes:

$ python3 savf_checksum_demo.py list edited-repaired.FILE
TESTB

$ python3 savf_checksum_demo.py fix edited-repaired.FILE edited-checked.FILE
checksum repaired: edited-checked.FILE

$ cmp -s edited-repaired.FILE edited-checked.FILE && echo "edited SAVF checksums valid"
edited SAVF checksums valid

$ wc -c baseline.FILE edited-repaired.FILE
152064 baseline.FILE
 84480 edited-repaired.FILE
236544 total

The repaired file is not a restored copy of the baseline: it is 128 records shorter, contains no TESTA item, and still contains the unchanged TESTB section payload.

The published editor intentionally emits only a checksum-repaired output. The edited-and-stale negative control described in the previous section was generated during validation by retaining the baseline global value while rebuilding the edited file’s record trailers. It isolates global-checksum enforcement, but deliberately creating invalid SAVFs is not part of the public command interface.

3. Import and inspect the edited SAVF

Upload the baseline and edited physical files through the same path:

scp baseline.FILE userb1@ibmi.example:/tmp/baseline.FILE
scp edited-repaired.FILE userb1@ibmi.example:/tmp/edited-repaired.FILE

Create separate SAVFs and import both files with CPYFRMSTMF:

CRTSAVF FILE(USERB1/BASEIN)
CRTSAVF FILE(USERB1/EDITFIX)

CPYFRMSTMF FROMSTMF('/tmp/baseline.FILE') TOMBR('/QSYS.LIB/USERB1.LIB/BASEIN.FILE') MBROPT(*REPLACE)
CPYFRMSTMF FROMSTMF('/tmp/edited-repaired.FILE') TOMBR('/QSYS.LIB/USERB1.LIB/EDITFIX.FILE') MBROPT(*REPLACE)

On the IBM i 7.5 system used for this article, both imports completed with CPCA081. The separately prepared stale control reported earlier failed with CPDA088 followed by CPFA095.

Display the repaired SAVF and restore its retained object into a fresh library:

DSPSAVF FILE(USERB1/EDITFIX) OUTPUT(*PRINT)
CRTLIB LIB(EDITTEST) TYPE(*TEST)
RSTOBJ OBJ(TESTB) SAVLIB(USERB1) DEV(*SAVF) OBJTYPE(*PGM) SAVF(USERB1/EDITFIX) RSTLIB(EDITTEST)

In the controlled run, DSPSAVF listed TESTB and did not list TESTA; RSTOBJ completed with CPC3703.

4. Other tool operations

The same release can copy one object from a compatible donor SAVF and can repair checksum fields without changing the saved-object data:

python3 savf_checksum_demo.py add target.FILE donor.FILE output.FILE OBJECT
python3 savf_checksum_demo.py fix input.FILE fixed.FILE

add requires compatible uncompressed catalogues, a unique donor object name, an unused descriptor slot, and enough free catalogue space. The repository README describes the supported layout and the conditions that make the command stop instead of guessing.

The security boundary

IBM’s record and global checks detect inconsistent or unrepaired SAVF data, but the values are deterministic and unkeyed. Once their algorithms are known, SAVFs using this layout can be verified, repaired, and structurally edited off-platform without using IBM i to regenerate the container checksums. This is useful for format tooling, forensic analysis, interoperability, and controlled repair of damaged SAVFs; it does not replace IBM i’s separate signature and saved-object validation mechanisms.

IBM documents a separate digital-signature layer for SAVFs. Program validation, object signatures, conversion, and restore-policy checks belong to the saved objects and restore process; they are separate from the SAVF container checksums and are not modified by the container repair. The final experiment avoids that ambiguity by removing one complete item while leaving the retained object’s saved section data unchanged.

Conclusion

The reverse engineering required two views of the same file: 528-byte physical records for the record trailers, and the concatenated 512-byte payloads for the logical stream. The per-record algorithm reduces a sequence number and payload through shifted byte-array additions and mixes in the SAVF timestamp. The global algorithm uses a 2,048-byte substitution table, two rotating states, counter-triggered shuffles, and a header backup to handle its overlay on the final payload.

The implementation reproduces all stored checksums in the original IBM-generated SAVF. Synthetic vectors exercise both algorithms, two nonzero-backup files confirm the role of the actual backup bytes in those examples, and the same table and nearby constants occur in IBM LIC media. The SAVE1/SAVE2 comparison also reconstructs a valid-record, stale-global state, showing exactly which checksum fields must be updated after a payload change.

The final IBM i control tested an actual container edit. I removed the complete TESTA item from a two-object, uncompressed SAVF, preserved TESTB’s saved-object section data, rebuilt the physical record stream, and regenerated the record and global checksum fields. IBM i rejected the structurally edited copy while its global value was stale. It accepted the repaired copy, DSPSAVF showed only TESTB, and TESTB restored successfully.

This establishes the checksum result for the tested IBM i 7.5 uncompressed QSYS layout: the SAVF container can be structurally edited and made internally valid again by recalculating its dependent checksum fields. It does not imply support for every historical or compressed SAVF variant, and it does not change IBM i’s separate signature or saved-object validation mechanisms.
content_text: Intro What exactly must be recalculated when bytes inside an IBM i save file are modified? IBM i save files, usually called SAVFs, use two container-consistency checksum mechanisms. Every 512-byte payload has a 16-byte trailer, and the logical stream also carries a 16-byte global checksum in its final payload. I wanted to understand both mechanisms well enough to reproduce them, modify a SAVF, and repair only the bytes that depended on my change. For the reconstruction, I used a small IBM-generated SAVF and the publicly distributed jSAVF reader, whose JAR I decompiled. I reimplemented both algorithms in Python and reproduced every stored checksum in the original file. A second file contained three changed payload bytes and a stale global checksum. Repairing that container changed only the global-checksum field and the final record trailer. I also found the global algorithm’s table and adjacent constants in IBM i Licensed Internal Code (LIC) installation media. Finally, I used the reconstructed format to remove one complete object from a two-object SAVF. A copy with valid record trailers but a stale global checksum was rejected during import. After I regenerated the global checksum and final trailer, IBM i accepted the shorter SAVF, DSPSAVF showed only the retained object, and that unchanged object restored successfully. These values provide internal consistency checks for the SAVF container, but they are deterministic, unkeyed, and recomputable. They do not authenticate the source or prevent somebody from modifying a file and recalculating its checksums. IBM i has separate mechanisms for SAVF signatures and for validating the objects stored inside the container. I will return to that boundary after the reversing work. Building a SAVF I could modify I wanted a small SAVF whose contents I controlled, so I created one containing a disposable program named USERB1/CALLAES. I disabled data compression because fixed, uncompressed payloads are much easier to compare byte for byte: CRTSAVF FILE(USERB1/SAVE1) SAVOBJ OBJ(CALLAES) LIB(USERB1) OBJTYPE(*PGM) DEV(*SAVF) SAVF(USERB1/SAVE1) DTACPR(*NO) CRTSAVF creates the save-file object. SAVOBJ saves the program into it, and DTACPR(*NO) keeps the data uncompressed. It does not disable either checksum layer. I copied the SAVF directly from /QSYS.LIB over SCP: scp userb1@ibmi.example:/QSYS.LIB/USERB1.LIB/SAVE1.FILE . The /QSYS.LIB/USERB1.LIB/SAVE1.FILE path is the Integrated File System view of the SAVF object. This transfer gives me a binary file that I can inspect byte for byte. The resulting SAVE1.FILE is 84,480 bytes long. What a SAVF looks like I did not have to discover the outer record format from scratch. A January 2001 MI400 post describes RISC SAVFs as 528-byte records: 512 data bytes, a four-byte binary record number, and a 12-byte checksum. A 2007 midrange.com discussion also describes checksum information in each 528-byte record. That layout fits my test file exactly: 84,480 bytes = 160 * 528 Each physical record contains a 512-byte payload followed by a 16-byte trailer: physical file: | 512-byte payload | 16-byte trailer | 512-byte payload | ... logical stream: | 512 payload bytes | 512 payload bytes Removing the trailers leaves an 81,920-byte logical stream: 81,920 bytes = 160 * 512 Once those trailers are removed, an offset inside the logical SAVF stream no longer matches the corresponding raw-file offset. I therefore use two coordinate systems: a physical offset addresses the transferred file, including the trailers; a logical offset addresses the concatenated 512-byte payloads. The conversion is: def logical_to_physical(offset: int) -> int: return (offset // 512) * 528 + (offset % 512) A modified copy named SAVE2.FILE appears later in the experiment. Its three payload differences from SAVE1.FILE show why this distinction matters: Logical offset Record index Offset in payload Physical offset 0x6D50 54 0x150 0x70B0 0x6D52 54 0x152 0x70B2 0x6D53 54 0x153 0x70B3 Here, index 54 means the zero-based record index. The trailer stores a one-based sequence, so the same unit is record #55. Hex editors and cmp use physical offsets; structures inside the SAVF use logical offsets. IBM also documents part of this outer layer. The CRTSAVF documentation says that retrieved SAVF records carry sequencing checksum information. IBM i validates it when records are inserted and rejects changed or out-of-sequence records. That documentation covers per-record insertion checks, not the global checksum discussed later. I did not run a separate live negative control for a corrupted record trailer. Record-level enforcement is documented by IBM; the controlled negative experiment later in this article isolates the second mechanism, the global checksum. Other public work already covered more than the outer layout. The initial 9 August 2026 revision of the Try-AS/400 SAVF page, preserved as revision 1781 in its page history, documented the per-record folding, timestamp XOR, global overlay, and backup at logical 0x40. It also documented the header-length and record-count fields, the item marker, name, catalogue reference, stored and total lengths, and the QSYS catalogue’s object count and descriptor layout used by the removal experiment below. The page warns that some material was generated or amended by AI and has not been checked, so I credit it as prior public documentation and validate the fields independently against my fixture and jSAVF. This article focuses on the complete global state-machine order, tests with nonzero backups, the matching LIC data, deterministic reconstruction and repair, public test vectors, and controlled IBM i behavior. Reconstructing the per-record checksum Instead of guessing standard checksum families, I looked for an existing SAVF reader. jSAVF already implemented the format, and its author credits information from the archive.midrange.com community, especially for IBM’s two proprietary checksum algorithms. I decompiled the distributed JAR and used its ChunkChecker logic as the starting point for the per-record algorithm. The first four bytes of each 16-byte trailer are the one-based record sequence. The remaining 12 bytes are the transformed checksum value. The values are easy to see in SAVE1.FILE: index 0 / record #1: 00000001 8f40b6a68e88a98ea91e2d60 index 1 / record #2: 00000002 af2012d24b4b7f2000004000 index 159 / record #160: 000000a0 afc501282b18f73c5c308e69 The decompiled code also uses the first eight bytes of the SAVF when building every record checksum. In SAVE1.FILE, those bytes are: af2012d24b4b7f20 jSAVF treats this value as the SAVF timestamp and mixes it into the checksum after the reduction passes. The main operation in the decompiled code is a shifted byte-array addition. jSAVF calls it chkAdd; the Python reconstruction below uses the name chk_add. The destination is one byte longer than the source: def chk_add(source: bytearray, destination: bytearray) -> None: shift_carry = 0 add_carry = 0 for i in range(len(source) - 1, -1, -1): value = source[i] shifted = ((value << 1) | shift_carry) & 0xff shift_carry = value >> 7 total = shifted + destination[i + 1] + add_carry add_carry = total >> 8 destination[i + 1] = total & 0xff destination[0] = ( destination[0] + add_carry + shift_carry ) & 0xff The source and destination are both big-endian bignums — the byte array is just one large number’s digits, most-significant byte first. chk_add doubles the source bignum (shift left by one bit) and adds it into the destination, which is one byte wider to hold any overflow. The bit that overflows out of the source’s top byte, plus the final carry from the addition, both land in destination[0]. The algorithm starts with the four-byte sequence followed by the 512-byte payload. It reduces those 516 bytes in two passes: Pass Input Buffer lengths Output 1 516 bytes 61 through 68 68 bytes 2 68 bytes 5 through 12 12 bytes Each pass fills eight buffers and then performs seven cascading chk_add operations. The unusual part is the order of the final two input slices. The first pass fills them in 68, 67 order, and the second uses 12, 11. The accumulator chain still runs through buffer indexes 0 to 7: def reduce_once(data: bytes, input_sizes: list[int]) -> bytes: parts = [] offset = 0 for size in input_sizes: parts.append(bytearray(data[offset:offset + size])) offset += size assert offset == len(data) # Earlier input fills buffer 7; the final input fills buffer 6. accumulators = parts[0:6] + [parts[7], parts[6]] for i in range(7): chk_add(accumulators[i], accumulators[i + 1]) return bytes(accumulators[7]) phase1_input = sequence.to_bytes(4, "big") + payload phase1 = reduce_once(phase1_input, [61, 62, 63, 64, 65, 66, 68, 67]) phase2 = reduce_once(phase1, [ 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 12, 11]) The last step XORs the first eight output bytes with the SAVF timestamp and prepends the sequence: result = bytearray(phase2) for i in range(8): result[i] ^= timestamp[i] record_checksum = sequence.to_bytes(4, "big") + bytes(result) Record #2 gives a compact test vector. Its 512-byte payload is entirely zero. With sequence 2 and timestamp af2012d24b4b7f20, the calculation produces: 00000002 af2012d24b4b7f2000004000 That is exactly the trailer stored in the IBM-generated file. Running the same calculation over all 160 records also reproduces every stored trailer. The zero payload is useful for checking the sequence handling and timestamp XOR, but it does not detect the unusual slice order. Both the correct order and a plain ascending fill produce the same zero-payload result. I therefore added a patterned record vector: payload = bytes(range(256)) * 2 sequence = 2 timestamp = bytes.fromhex("af2012d24b4b7f20") The correct 68,67 and 12,11 fill order produces: 000000028e43fa214379304d4081df91 Filling the last two buffers in plain ascending order instead produces: 0000000272b71b3df71e6c4d4081df3f I checked the correct result directly with jSAVF 1.83’s compiled ChunkChecker, as well as with the public Python implementation used below. This vector catches the ordering error without exposing any bytes from the test SAVF. Finding the global checksum Fixing the record trailers was not enough. jSAVF’s GlobalChecker showed a second 16-byte value calculated over the complete logical stream. The field sits in the final 16 logical bytes. Physically, those are the last 16 bytes of the final record’s payload, immediately before its record trailer: | 496 ordinary payload bytes | 16-byte global checksum | 16-byte record trailer | ^ file_size - 32 ^ file_size - 16 For my 84,480-byte file, the global field begins at 0x149E0 (84,448) and the final record trailer begins at 0x149F0 (84,464). This creates a self-reference problem: the global checksum occupies bytes that would otherwise be part of its own input. In the decompiled code, GlobalChecker solves it by reading the original 16 bytes from logical offset 0x40 in the first payload. To calculate the global value, I restore that backup over the final field, process the reconstructed logical stream, and then write the checksum back into the final payload. The global routine uses a 2,048-byte lookup table. jSAVF stores it as net/anerty/os400/savf/check/sandbox.ser inside the JAR. The file is a serialized Java byte array, 2,075 bytes long, with the actual table beginning at offset 27: ac ed 00 05 75 72 ... 00 00 08 00 <2,048-byte payload> ^ stream magic ^ length = 0x800 The table hash is: 2,048-byte table SHA-256: 93f81fd81523a2521cf17b234edb05155998bc7e46d88b966b4bd9eef64c0764 The table contains eight 256-byte blocks. Each block is a permutation of 00 through ff, so every byte value occurs eight times in the complete table. I checked the current jSAVF 1.83 distribution and extracted the same resource with these commands: curl -fL -A 'Mozilla/5.0' -O https://www.anerty.net/dl/jsavf-dist-1.83-jars-only-linux.tar.xz tar -xJf jsavf-dist-1.83-jars-only-linux.tar.xz unzip -p jsavf/jSAVF-1.83.jar net/anerty/os400/savf/check/sandbox.ser > sandbox.ser The global state starts with two eight-byte values and two counters: s0 = bytearray([0x55] * 8) s8 = bytearray([0xaa] * 8) c0 = 1 c8 = 121 Each 512-byte payload is processed as 32 blocks of 16 bytes. The first eight bytes update s0, and the second eight update s8. Each half is treated as a ring of 8 bytes rather than a flat list, so every byte has a neighbor to its right and byte 7 wraps back around to byte 0: b0 → b1 → b2 → b3 ↑ ↓ b7 ← b6 ← b5 ← b4 Reading clockwise from b7, each adjacent pair feeds one table lookup: (b7,b0) → state[0], (b0,b1) → state[1], … (b6,b7) → state[7]. The routine builds this ring by prepending a copy of the last byte, giving a nine-byte window, then folds each adjacent pair into an 11-bit table index: window = bytes([half[7]]) + half for k in range(8): index = ((window[k] << 8) | window[k + 1]) & 0x7ff state[k] ^= table[index] After the table XOR, the eight-byte state rotates left by 29 bits as one unsigned big-endian 64-bit value. When the s0 counter reaches 251 or the s8 counter reaches 257, the corresponding state is shuffled at bit level. An s8 threshold event also exchanges bytes 4 through 7 between the two states. The following pseudocode includes all state and ordering needed to reproduce the checksum. physical is the complete SAVF image and table is the 2,048-byte lookup table. The function derives the ordered 512-byte payload blocks by stripping the 16-byte physical trailer from each 528-byte record: MASK64 = (1 << 64) - 1 def rotate_left_64_be(state: bytearray, count: int = 29) -> None: value = int.from_bytes(state, "big", signed=False) value = ((value << count) | (value >> (64 - count))) & MASK64 state[:] = value.to_bytes(8, "big") def build_spread_tables(): spread1 = [0] * 256 for byte in range(256): value = 0 for bit in range(7, -1, -1): value = (value << 2) | ((byte >> bit) & 1) spread1[byte] = value spread2 = [(value << 1) & 0xffff for value in spread1] return spread1, spread2 def shuffle(state, spread1, spread2): output = bytearray(8) for pair in range(4): value = spread2[state[pair]] | spread1[state[pair + 4]] output[pair * 2:pair * 2 + 2] = value.to_bytes(2, "big") state[:] = output def mix_half(half, state, counter, threshold, table, spread1, spread2): window = bytes([half[7]]) + bytes(half) for k in range(8): index = ((window[k] << 8) | window[k + 1]) & 0x7ff state[k] ^= table[index] rotate_left_64_be(state, 29) threshold_event = (counter == threshold) if threshold_event: counter = 0 shuffle(state, spread1, spread2) # The caller performs the cross-state exchange, if required, # before incrementing this counter. return counter, threshold_event def compute_global_checksum(physical: bytes, table: bytes) -> bytes: assert len(physical) > 0 and len(physical) % 528 == 0 assert len(table) == 2048 records = [ physical[i * 528:i * 528 + 512] for i in range(len(physical) // 528) ] spread1, spread2 = build_spread_tables() s0 = bytearray([0x55] * 8) s8 = bytearray([0xaa] * 8) c0, c8 = 1, 121 global_backup = records[0][0x40:0x50] for record_index, record in enumerate(records): payload = bytearray(record) if record_index == len(records) - 1: payload[496:512] = global_backup for offset in range(0, 512, 16): block = payload[offset:offset + 16] c0, _ = mix_half( block[0:8], s0, c0, 251, table, spread1, spread2 ) c0 += 1 c8, s8_event = mix_half( block[8:16], s8, c8, 257, table, spread1, spread2 ) if s8_event: old_s0_tail = bytes(s0[4:8]) s0[4:8] = s8[4:8] s8[4:8] = old_s0_tail c8 += 1 return bytes(s0) + bytes(s8) build_spread_tables implements a classic bit-interleaving trick: spread1[byte] spreads the 8 bits of byte out so each bit lands in every other bit position of a 16-bit value, leaving the in-between positions zero; spread2 is the same table shifted left by one bit, so its bits land exactly in the positions spread1 left empty: bit position: 15 14 13 12 11 10 09 08 07 06 05 04 03 02 01 00 spread1(byte): 0 b7 0 b6 0 b5 0 b4 0 b3 0 b2 0 b1 0 b0 spread2(byte): b7 0 b6 0 b5 0 b4 0 b3 0 b2 0 b1 0 b0 0 shuffle then combines one byte from each half of the state — spread2[state[pair]] from the first half, spread1[state[pair + 4]] from the second — by OR-ing their spread values together, interleaving the two bytes’ bits pairwise into one 16-bit output. Doing this for all four byte pairs interleaves the state’s two four-byte halves together, bit by bit. The order matters. The algorithm first applies the table XOR and rotates the result by 29 bits. It then tests the counter. If the counter has reached its limit, the algorithm resets it and shuffles the bits. For s8, it also exchanges four bytes between the two running values. Only then does it increment the counter. Changing this order changes the result. A synthetic global-checksum vector The following vector tests the global algorithm without a private SAVF. It contains nine physical records. Payload byte i in zero-based record r is (r * 17 + i * 29 + 3) & 0xff. The backup at logical 0x40 is f0f1...feff, the final overlay initially contains a0a1...aeaf, and each 16-byte physical trailer is zero because trailers are not global-checksum input. Nine records contain 288 blocks, so this vector reaches both shuffle thresholds and the s8-triggered cross-state exchange: records = [] for record_index in range(9): payload = bytearray( (record_index * 17 + offset * 29 + 3) & 0xff for offset in range(512) ) records.append(payload) records[0][0x40:0x50] = bytes(range(0xf0, 0x100)) records[-1][496:512] = bytes(range(0xa0, 0xb0)) physical = bytearray() for payload in records: physical.extend(payload) physical.extend(bytes(16)) expected = bytes.fromhex("dbf1671ed17396a03f60bd52ddf749db") calculated = compute_global_checksum(bytes(physical), table) assert calculated == expected print(f"calculated global: {calculated.hex()}") The output is: calculated global: dbf1671ed17396a03f60bd52ddf749db The lookup table has the SHA-256 shown above. I checked this expected value directly with jSAVF 1.83’s compiled GlobalChecker and with the independent Python reconstruction. Why the final record must be repaired last Writing the global checksum changes the final record’s payload and invalidates that record’s trailer. For an ordinary payload edit, the dependencies are: changed payload bytes +-> affected record trailer(s) `-> global checksum `-> final record trailer The global calculation reads only the 512-byte payloads, not the physical record trailers. The affected trailer and the global value are therefore parallel results of the payload change. The final trailer depends on the newly written global value and must be calculated last. A safe repair order is: recalculate the record trailers; calculate the global value after restoring the header backup over the final field; write the global value at file_size - 32; recalculate the final record trailer again. There is one special case. The global field physically replaces the true final 16 logical bytes. If those bytes must change, the replacement data belongs in the backup at logical 0x40. That changes record #1’s payload and trailer, the global checksum, and finally the last record’s trailer. Testing the backup assumption The SAVFs used in the main experiment had zero-filled backups at logical 0x40. This meant that an implementation which replaced the final field with zeroes would still produce the correct result for those files. I therefore looked for SAVFs with a nonzero backup and found two useful examples: File Backup at logical 0x40 Stored global Zero-filled calculation Backup-aware calculation 20260830_QSYS_QTOCSSTBL_uncompressed.savf 40404040404040404040404040404040 d1d0d5c608257c3a75f62b1d3b509364 11101506c8e5bcfab536ebddfb9053a4 exact match QTOFRULZ.FILE d3404040404000000000000000000000 59311393322093c8527e36d903e5c4a4 99f1d393395a1308527e36d903e5c4a4 exact match Both files also have valid per-record trailers. Replacing the overlaid field with zeroes produces the wrong values shown in the table. Restoring the 16-byte header backup reproduces each stored global checksum exactly. For these two files, this confirms that the backup is part of the global-checksum input. Finding the same constants in IBM LIC jSAVF showed how the global checksum was calculated. I also wanted to see whether the same unusual table and constants appeared in IBM’s LIC. I searched an IBM i 7.5 RS_750-J Licensed Machine Code installation image for the complete 2,048-byte table. It occurs once in the installation image, at offset 0x42FDE8A0. Within the 64 bytes immediately before the table, I found the two state seeds, both counter seeds, and both thresholds used by the reconstructed algorithm: 0x42FDE860: 55555555 55555555 00000000 00000000 initial s0 0x42FDE870: 00000001 000000fb 00000000 00000000 c0 = 1, threshold = 251 0x42FDE880: aaaaaaaa aaaaaaaa 00000000 00000000 initial s8 0x42FDE890: 00000079 00000101 00000000 00000000 c8 = 121, threshold = 257 0x42FDE8A0: 90aca3f7 e3e620be 686e0935 ea4efd6c table begins The same table is present in QFILEMCD, an extracted LIC code-and-data image. It begins at file offset 0x2503E8A0. If you have access to licensed IBM LIC installation media and an extracted QFILEMCD, the table search itself is straightforward: from pathlib import Path import hashlib import mmap EXPECTED_TABLE_SHA256 = ( "93f81fd81523a2521cf17b234edb05155998bc7e46d88b966b4bd9eef64c0764" ) table_resource = Path("sandbox.ser").read_bytes() assert len(table_resource) >= 27 + 2048 table = table_resource[27:27 + 2048] # Pin the table extracted from the jSAVF 1.83 build used for this article. assert hashlib.sha256(table).hexdigest() == EXPECTED_TABLE_SHA256 with open("QFILEMCD", "rb") as f, \ mmap.mmap(f.fileno(), 0, access=mmap.ACCESS_READ) as image: offsets, start = [], 0 while (found := image.find(table, start)) != -1: offsets.append(found) start = found + 1 print([hex(offset) for offset in offsets]) On the QFILEMCD image I analyzed, the output was: ['0x2503e8a0'] This locates one complete copy of the table at the file offset given above. Finding the constants does not identify the LIC routine that reads them or prove that IBM’s control flow matches jSAVF. It also does not show that the machine which created my SAVF ran this exact LIC level. The search shows that IBM’s installation media contains the same table together with the matching state seeds, counter seeds, and thresholds. Modifying and repairing the SAVF I put the backup-aware implementation in a standalone Python script named savf_checksum_demo.py. Its public interface has four operations: repair the checksum fields, list saved objects, copy an object from a compatible donor SAVF, and remove an object. The add and remove operations repair every dependent checksum field automatically. The reproduction section below uses the same object-removal path as the final experiment without requiring private files. Validating against the original SAVF I ran the reconstruction on the untouched IBM-generated file. The validation output was: record trailers: all 160 OK stored global: 5513f83d38b944fe9814e1dc8d0b04fe calculated global: 5513f83d38b944fe9814e1dc8d0b04fe global checksum: OK The Python implementation reproduces all 160 record trailers and the stored global value 5513f83d38b944fe9814e1dc8d0b04fe. This checks the record numbering, both reduction passes, timestamp XOR, table parsing, field placement, and global state transitions against values written by IBM i. Analyzing a valid-record, stale-global file SAVE2.FILE gave me a useful intermediate state. Compared with SAVE1.FILE, three program payload bytes in record #55 (index 54) changed to 0x41: Logical offset Physical offset Change 0x6D50 0x70B0 fb to 41 0x6D52 0x70B2 ff to 41 0x6D53 0x70B3 30 to 41 Five bytes in record #55’s trailer changed with the payload. The updated trailer matches those bytes, and all 160 record trailers are valid. The global checksum and the final record trailer are still byte-for-byte equal to SAVE1.FILE, so the stored global value is stale. record trailers: all 160 OK stored global: 5513f83d38b944fe9814e1dc8d0b04fe calculated global: 5013b87d388154fb9835f5dc8d0980ff global checksum: STALE Compared with SAVE1.FILE, this intermediate file differs at eight positions: the three payload bytes and five bytes in record #55’s trailer. I recreated this state by applying those three edits to SAVE1.FILE and recalculating only record #55’s trailer; the result matched SAVE2.FILE byte for byte. Predicting the repair footprint The dependency model predicts that repairing SAVE2.FILE should change only two places: the embedded global field; the final record trailer, because the global field is part of its payload. The changed program bytes and record #55 trailer should remain untouched. I repaired a copy with the final tool: $ python3 savf_checksum_demo.py fix SAVE2.FILE SAVE2-repaired.FILE checksum repaired: SAVE2-repaired.FILE A separate validation pass found all 160 record trailers valid and both the stored and calculated global value equal to 5013b87d388154fb9835f5dc8d0980ff. cmp finds exactly 21 changed byte positions between SAVE2.FILE and the repaired output: physical 0x149E0..0x149EF global field: 11 positions differ physical 0x149F0..0x149FF final record trailer: 10 positions differ elsewhere: 0 differences Only 11 and 10 positions differ because some bytes happen to be equal in the old and new 16-byte values. The complete comparison is: Comparison Payload bytes Trailer bytes Global-field bytes Total positions SAVE1.FILE to SAVE2.FILE 3 5 in record #55 0 8 SAVE2.FILE to repaired output 0 10 in record #160 11 21 SAVE1.FILE to repaired output 3 15 across two trailers 11 29 This is a consistency check rather than an independent validation, because the same implementation both predicts and produces the repair. Still, the output changes only the expected 21 byte positions and nothing else. Editing a SAVF container The three-byte SAVE1/SAVE2 comparison established the checksum dependency order, but editing bytes inside a saved program also raises unrelated object-validation questions. For the final test I therefore changed the SAVF structure instead: I removed one complete object from a two-object container and left the retained object’s saved section data unchanged. I created TESTA and TESTB as disposable copies of the same program and saved them together without compression. The resulting SAVF had 288 physical records. Its backup-restored logical stream contained three sequential items. Here, an item is one continuous area of bytes with its own header and stored length: QSRDSSPC.1 logical 0x1000..0x3fff length 0x3000 srds 0x0 TESTA logical 0x4000..0x13fff length 0x10000 srds 0x70 TESTB logical 0x14000..0x23fff length 0x10000 srds 0x107 In this output, srds is the QSYS catalogue-descriptor offset encoded in the low 24 bits of the item field at +0x24 (zero for the catalogue item itself). A descriptor is the catalogue entry for one saved object. These offsets come from three different structures, each relative to its own start rather than to the whole file: logical stream ├─ file header (+0x34 header length, +0x08/+0x38 record count) ├─ QSRDSSPC.1 item 0x1000..0x3fff │ ├─ item header (+0x04 name, +0x24 catalogue-descriptor link) │ └─ catalogue (+0x2A object count) │ ├─ descriptor[0] @ +0x70 (151 bytes — TESTA) │ └─ descriptor[1] @ +0x107 (151 bytes — TESTB) ├─ TESTA item 0x4000..0x13fff (item header +0x24 → 0x70) └─ TESTB item 0x14000..0x23fff (item header +0x24 → 0x107) With that in mind: QSRDSSPC.1 is the save/restore data-space item that carries the object catalogue. The parser restores the global overlay before walking the logical stream. The four-byte big-endian header-length field at 0x34 was 0x1000, so the first item began at logical 0x1000. The implementation also supports the documented zero value, which means a 512-byte header. It checks the 0xFFFFFFFF item marker, reads the EBCDIC name at item offset 0x04, and calculates each uncompressed item’s stored length from the four-byte big-endian field at 0x48: (big_endian_u32(item + 0x48) + 1) * 512 The item also stores its total length, in 512-byte units, in the four-byte big-endian field at 0xCC. The 2001 MI400 description calls this the number of 528-byte records to the next descriptor. Both descriptions agree for contiguous non-final items: the same count describes both views. Multiplying it by 512 gives the item’s logical length, while the same number of 528-byte physical records gives the raw-file distance to the next descriptor. The final item still carries its total length even though no descriptor follows it. For this fixture, QSRDSSPC.1 stored 0x17 at 0x48 and 0x18 at 0xCC; both derive a length of 0x3000. TESTA and TESTB each stored 0x7F at 0x48 and 0x80 at 0xCC; both derive 0x10000. These values equal the actual item spans. There is no separate absolute next-item pointer in this QSYS layout: the outer parser advances by the computed item length, while the object catalogue is a count-delimited, fixed-stride descriptor array. jSAVF’s separate next-item handling is for IFS catalogue trees, which are not present here. Removing TESTA did not require changing 0xCC: QSRDSSPC.1 kept its 0x3000 span, and the retained TESTB item moved earlier but kept its 0x10000 span. The editor changed the four-byte big-endian record count at header offset 0x08 and the matching eight-byte big-endian count at 0x38 from 288 to 160; the header-length field remained 0x1000. The catalogue occupies logical 0x3000..0x3FFF. Its four-byte big-endian object count at catalogue offset 0x2A was two. For this target-release format, the two 151-byte object descriptors began at catalogue offsets 0x70 and 0x107. Each saved-object item contains a four-byte big-endian field at item offset 0x24. jSAVF uses the high byte for IFS flags and the low 24 bits as the QSYS catalogue-descriptor offset; the QSYS values here were 0x70 and 0x107. Removing TESTA therefore required more than deleting its bytes. The editor: removed the complete TESTA item at 0x4000..0x13FFF; changed the catalogue object count from two to one; moved the TESTB descriptor from 0x107 to 0x70 and cleared the unused slot; changed TESTB’s item-header descriptor link from 0x107 to 0x70; updated both record-count fields in the file header; copied the new final 16 logical bytes to the backup at logical 0x40, rebuilt the physical records, and recalculated every record trailer; calculated the new global checksum, wrote it to the final payload, and recalculated the final trailer. The 151-byte TESTB catalogue descriptor was copied unchanged from 0x107 to 0x70. Its header occupation at item offset 0x44 was 0x2F8; its saved-object sections began at the first 4096-byte boundary, item-relative 0x1000. After aligning the baseline and edited TESTB items, the only differences in that first 0x1000-byte descriptor/header area were relative offsets 0x26 and 0x27, inside the four-byte catalogue-reference field. Every byte from item offset 0x1000 through the end of the item was unchanged. The edit produced these structural changes: Property Baseline Edited TESTA item 0x4000..0x13FFF absent TESTB item 0x14000..0x23FFF 0x4000..0x13FFF Logical size 0x24000 (147,456 bytes) 0x14000 (81,920 bytes) Physical records 288 160 Physical size 152,064 bytes 84,480 bytes Stored global checksum 791ea5ec90f35d20829dc5561098c130 bfd84cce59a6e7993e85c8a0e1a4e9cf For this fixture the new final logical bytes and the backup were both zero. The implementation nevertheless copies the actual new tail into the backup rather than assuming zeroes. Before import, the repaired result satisfied these invariants: SAVF differs from baseline: YES logical structure differs: YES TESTA present in baseline: YES TESTA present in edited: NO TESTB present in baseline: YES TESTB present in edited: YES TESTB saved-object section payload changed: NO TESTB item-header descriptor link: 0x107 -> 0x70 record trailers: all 160 OK stored global == calculated global: YES I also generated a negative control with the same structural edit and rebuilt record trailers, but left the old global value in place. Its 160 trailers all validated; its stored global was 791ea5ec90f35d20829dc5561098c130, while the calculation produced bfd84cce59a6e7993e85c8a0e1a4e9cf. The stale and repaired copies have identical backup-restored logical streams. Their 28 differing physical byte positions are confined to the global field at 0x149E0..0x149EF and the final record trailer at 0x149F0..0x149FF. Testing the edited SAVF on IBM i I transferred the baseline, edited-and-stale, and edited-and-repaired files through the same stream-file and CPYFRMSTMF path on IBM i 7.5. The baseline and edited variants used separate destination SAVFs, and each restore used a fresh target library. Case Record checks Global CPYFRMSTMF DSPSAVF Restore TESTB Baseline 288 valid valid CPCA081 TESTA, TESTB CPC3703 Edited + stale 160 valid stale CPDA088, then CPFA095 not reached not reached Edited + repaired 160 valid valid CPCA081 TESTB only CPC3703 The stale import stopped with: CPDA088: Error writing to object. CPFA095: Stream file not copied. The repaired import completed with: CPCA081: Stream file copied to object. DSPSAVF reported 160 records, one saved object, and listed only TESTB. Restoring that retained object into an empty library produced: CPC3703: 1 objects restored from SVC29 to RMRF29. The actual controlled run used SVC29 as the source library and RMRF29 as the fresh restore library; the reproduction commands below use generic example names. This is the practical checksum-fixer result. The SAVF was structurally different, TESTA was absent, and TESTB’s saved-object section data had not changed. After the dependent record and global checksum fields were regenerated, IBM i accepted and interpreted the edited container, and the retained object remained usable. The editor is not intended to reproduce the byte-for-byte output of a fresh native SAVOBJ operation; the experiment tests whether the structurally edited and checksum-repaired container is accepted and interpreted correctly by IBM i. Reproducing the experiment The private research SAVFs are not required. The specific implementation used for these experiments is available in the Silent Signal SAVF IBM i repository. It requires Python 3.9 or later and exposes four commands: fix recalculates every record trailer, the global checksum, and the final trailer; list validates the record trailers and lists the QSYS catalogue; add copies one complete object from a compatible donor SAVF and repairs the output; and remove removes one complete object and repairs the output. The editor deliberately supports the uncompressed QSYS layout tested here. It rejects compressed items, incompatible catalogues, ambiguous names, unknown links, and insufficient catalogue space rather than guessing. First extract the lookup-table resource from the public jSAVF distribution: curl -fL -A 'Mozilla/5.0' -O https://www.anerty.net/dl/jsavf-dist-1.83-jars-only-linux.tar.xz tar -xJf jsavf-dist-1.83-jars-only-linux.tar.xz unzip -p jsavf/jSAVF-1.83.jar net/anerty/os400/savf/check/sandbox.ser > sandbox.ser Every checksum-changing command validates the extracted table against the SHA-256 published earlier in this article before using it. 1. Create and export a two-object baseline Replace USERB1 with a disposable test library and TESTPGM with a disposable program that can be duplicated. The SSH account and host below are examples.
